paragraphs.text: Listen First
Moses Afolabi
Work through these eight chapters with a
notebook or a practice partner. Try one
exercise in a real conversation, then return
to what the other person actually said and
what you learned.
1 Make room for the whole story
Read James 1:19–20. James connects a
readiness to hear with restraint in speech
and anger. Those instructions meet us at
the moment we are sure we already
understand. A spouse starts explaining why
the week has felt heavy, and our minds
race to the chores we completed. A church
volunteer describes what went wrong, and
we begin assembling a defense of the
schedule. We can hear every word while
preparing to answer a different question.
CHAPTER 1 · LISTENING IN PRACTICE
Make room for the whole story
Lagos, Nigeria. A father puts his phone down before his daughter speaks.
I’m listening. What made the ride home difficult today?
Could we talk after I’ve had some quiet?
Give the speaker control over the pace.
Try putting down what is in your hands and
giving the person a complete turn. When
they pause, leave a breath before
responding. They may be thinking, trying to
decide whether it is safe to say more, or
simply looking for the next word. If you are
distracted by an urgent task, agree on a
time you can actually give them your
attention. “I can sit with you after I finish
this call. Would seven o’clock work?” Then
keep the appointment.
Family practice. A teenager says, “I don’t
want to go back.” Begin with “What
happened that makes going back hard?” As
they tell the story, notice the moment you
want to interrupt. Write down afterward
what became clear because you waited. If
the person raises an immediate safety
concern, respond to that concern and
arrange appropriate help.
Prayer. Lord, give me patience to hear my
neighbor fully. Help me notice when I am preparing a defense, and give me the humility to ask what I have missed. Amen.
Notice how you enter a conversation
When you arrive tired, even a simple
request can feel like one more task. Name
what you can do. “I want to give you my
attention. Can we sit down after dinner?”
An agreed time is useful only if you return.
Set a reminder and keep your word. If a
person is raising an urgent concern, give it
attention now and find support as needed.
Consider a family member who says you
have been distant. You may remember a
long week of errands performed on their
behalf. Ask which moments made them feel
the distance. They may describe trying to
share something important while you were
reading messages at the table. You can
acknowledge the moment without trying to
settle the whole relationship in one sitting.
“I was looking at my phone when you tried to tell me. I can see why it felt like I had tuned out.”
When the opening line hides the real concern
At the end of a shift, a parent hears, “You
always ask me how school was when I get
in the car.” The familiar question was
intended as an invitation. The teenager
experiences it as one more demand before
they have had a moment to settle. The
parent can defend their intention and still
miss the useful information. Try, “Would
you rather have some quiet on the way
home, or is there a different time you’d
actually like to talk?” Wait for an answer
the parent did not choose.
Listening requires decisions about attention
as well as words. Set down the object in
your hand. Turn off the television if others
are willing. Sit where you can both hear. If
time is limited, name the amount of time
available and offer to return at a specific hour. These actions create a better opening for the conversation. They do not require the other person to explain everything at once.
Imagine the teenager says they would
rather walk the dog together after dinner.
At that point, leave the question about
school alone and keep the invitation to
walk. If they choose to tell you more
outside, the change of setting has helped. If
they say little, the walk still gives you a
chance to spend time together. Choose a
household conversation where changing
the setting would make more difference
than asking a clever question.
Make time to hear
Phone down Give a turn Return as agreed
A quieter setting can make room for a fuller answer.
2 Ask questions the speaker can answer
Read Proverbs 18:13 and 18:17. An early
account can sound complete because we fill
in what we do not yet know. A question
helps when it gives the person room to
supply a detail you could not see. “What
happened after the meeting?” opens that
room. “Why did you get so worked up?”
already supplies an interpretation.
Use the speaker’s own words to locate the
place where more detail would help. If a
volunteer says they were left out, ask which
decision they expected to be part of. If a
colleague says the deadline was unfair, ask
when they learned what was due and what
else was already on their schedule. One
well-placed question gives the speaker time
to answer thoughtfully.
There is room for a direct question when a
concrete detail matters. “Did you receive
CHAPTER 2 · LISTENING IN PRACTICE
Ask questions the speaker can answer
Nairobi, Kenya. A church newcomer points to the doorway where she lost her way.
Where were you when you first weren’t sure which way to go?
At the door from the parking lot. I couldn’t see room signs.
Ask where the problem began before suggesting a fix.
the updated schedule before Sunday?” can
establish a fact. Follow it with a question
about the effect. “What did the late notice
change for you?” The first answer helps you
understand the sequence. The second helps
you understand why it mattered.
Workbook exercise. Turn each assumption
into an open question.
They ignored the message. — What
information did you have before you made
the decision?
They are upset about the new leader. —
Which part of the change concerns you
most?
They just want someone to solve it. — What
would be helpful from me today?
Write one assumption of your own. Practice
asking the revised question aloud. Remove
any word that presumes the other person’s
motive.
Slow down when several people disagree
At a ministry planning meeting, two
volunteers say the refreshment budget was
approved and a third says it was discussed
as a possibility. Ask each person what they
heard and when. Read back the point of
agreement first. Then identify the disputed
detail and check the minutes or ask the
person who had authority to approve it. If
the answer is still unclear, decide who will
confirm it and when. This keeps people
from having to defend their character over
a question about process.
A good follow-up question has a purpose
the speaker can understand. “Who else was
there?” may sound like a challenge if they
have just shared something painful. Explain
your reason where appropriate. “I want to
understand who had the information when
the decision was made. Who was at that
meeting?” Give the speaker room to say
they do not remember.
Rehearsal. Take one question you regularly
ask a spouse, colleague, or volunteer. Write
down what you hope to learn and check
whether your wording leaves room for two
different answers. Practice a follow-up
based on what they actually say.
A question that leaves room for two answers
A colleague says the new schedule has
made their day more difficult. “You don’t
like the new hours, do you?” gives them
your explanation before they can offer
theirs. Ask which part of the day became
harder. The difficulty may be the time, the
change in duties, or a lack of information. In
your notebook, draft a question with a
guessed explanation and rewrite it so the
person can supply one you had not thought
of.
Find which question belongs next
A newcomer at church says it took a long
time to find the right room. A volunteer
responds, “Did you read the sign?” That
question can establish whether the sign
was seen, but it does not yet show where
the route stopped making sense. A more
useful opening is, “Where were you when
you first realized you weren’t sure which
way to go?” The newcomer remembers that
the door from the parking lot had no room
labels. The volunteer now has a better
problem to fix.
Different questions do different jobs. A
question about sequence helps you
reconstruct what happened. A question
about effect helps you hear which
consequence mattered. A question about
preference helps you learn what the person
would choose next time. Ask for sequence
first if there is a dispute about facts. When
someone is hurting, you may need to hear the effect before either of you is ready to reconstruct the sequence.
Practice by writing down a problem another
person mentioned this week. Draft one
question for each of those three jobs.
Choose the one that the person could
answer without first accepting your
explanation. In a real conversation, allow an
answer to change the order. For example,
an important effect may reveal a different
event to ask about.
3 Reflect what you heard and invite correction
Read Philippians 2:3–4. Reflecting what you
heard helps you attend to another person’s
interests. Summarize the part they
emphasized and let them correct it. If you
infer an emotion, offer your reading gently.
“It sounds like you felt sidelined when the
decision went out before you were asked.
Have I understood?” One short summary
often gives the speaker a clearer chance to
confirm or correct you than a long speech
about what they must be feeling.
Suppose the volunteer says, “I was relieved
to have less responsibility. I just needed
someone to tell me before people started
calling.” Take the correction as useful
information. You can say, “So the issue was
finding out late, especially once people
began asking you questions.” A workable
response may now be a smaller change to
how the team communicates.
CHAPTER 3 · LISTENING IN PRACTICE
Reflect what you heard
Shenzhen, China. Two coworkers look at an invoice and clarify what information was missing.
Were you worried about having to promise the wrong total?
Yes. I needed the approved figures before answering.
Let the speaker correct what you inferred.
Reflect meaning without making assumptions about feelings
People express discomfort in different
ways. Looking away can signal thought,
distraction, or a preference for less eye
contact. Treat body language as a reason to
check in. “Would it help to slow down or
take a minute?” gives the speaker a choice.
During a phone conversation, ask whether
a long pause means they are thinking or
whether the connection dropped.
Use the facts you heard as anchors. A
coworker says the plan changed twice and
they found out from a customer. A useful
reflection might be, “You were expected to
explain a policy you hadn’t received.” If the
person says they were mainly concerned
about being unable to help the customer,
repeat that in the next response. You can
then talk about how updates reach the
people who answer questions.
Three-minute practice. With a willing
partner, listen for one minute while they
describe an ordinary frustration. Spend the
second minute reflecting one fact and one
concern. Give them the third minute to
correct you. Ask which part you
remembered accurately and which word
changed what they meant.
Check the part that matters
A friend describes missing a gathering and
says they were upset. You reflect that they
were upset at being left out. They explain
that they needed advance notice to arrange
a ride. Repeat the transport issue and ask
whether a message the day before would
help. Practice ending your reflection with a
short check rather than a long explanation.
Ask your practice partner to correct one
detail you deliberately made tentative.
Check which part you have understood
At work, a colleague complains that they
were asked to explain an invoice they had
never seen. You reply, “It was embarrassing
to be corrected in front of a customer.”
They say, “The customer was patient. I was
worried I’d promise something we couldn’t
deliver.” Thank them for correcting you.
The next question belongs to the risk they
identified: “What figures would you need
before making that promise?” You now
have a concrete operational problem to
resolve.
When you reflect, choose one sentence you
can say without borrowing the speaker’s
emotion as your own. “You were asked to
give an answer before you had the invoice.”
If their concern appears clear, add it as a
question: “Was the concern that you might
give the wrong total?” That phrasing gives
them room to correct a detail without
rejecting the whole response.
Practice listening for the difference
between the person’s request and the
reason they give. Someone may ask for
more notice and explain they need time to
find childcare. The action is earlier notice.
The reason reveals how early might be
useful. If you hear only that they were
disappointed, you may offer sympathy and
leave the practical concern unresolved.
Check your reading
Words heard Meaning checked Reply adjusted
The speaker can correct your interpretation before you respond.
4 Listen under pressure
Read Proverbs 15:1 and Ephesians 4:15.
Gentleness leaves room for a truthful
answer. It also shapes how you respond
when someone’s account of an event
conflicts with yours.
At a team meeting, a staff member says,
“We always find out after the decision is
made.” Begin with a specific example.
“Which decision felt that way this week?”
Listen long enough to identify what can be
verified. “The schedule had already gone
out before I asked for input. I can see why
that question felt pointless.” If something
remains open to discussion, state what it is.
“The dates are fixed. We can still change
who covers the first hour. Is that where
your suggestion would help?”
When a conversation gets heated, set a
boundary that you can keep. “I want to
hear you, and I need us to stop calling each
other names. Can we pause for ten minutes
CHAPTER 4 · LISTENING IN PRACTICE
Listen under pressure
São Paulo, Brazil. Two volunteers compare what they understood about the supply budget.
I thought this amount was for today’s supplies. How did you read the note?
I thought it was for the whole weekend. Let’s check before we spend it.
Clarify the difference before deciding what to change.
and try again?” If taking a pause is possible,
agree on when you will return. Where there
are threats or abuse, prioritize safety and
seek appropriate support. Listening can
help you understand a situation while you
make a clear decision about what behavior
you can safely accept.
Pair exercise. Take turns raising a realistic
complaint. Each listener asks for a specific
example, summarizes the concern, and
states one fact or next step. Switch roles.
Afterward, ask your partner which words
made it easier to tell the truth.
Repair a conversation you handled poorly
Suppose you interrupted a team member
and said their concern was minor. When
you have time to speak privately, name the
action specifically. “I interrupted you and
called the concern minor before I
understood it. I’d like to hear the rest if
you’re willing.” If they are willing, offer a
time and give them a complete turn. If they
need time, respect their decision and revisit
the issue through an appropriate channel if
work still depends on it.
When the concern is accurate, make a
commitment you can describe plainly. “I’ll
send the new schedule by Wednesday
afternoon and ask for conflicts before
Friday.” When you disagree about part of
the story, explain what you remember and
seek a shared record. People can disagree
about what happened and still agree on
how information will be communicated next
time.
Reflection on Ephesians 4:15. Write down a
truth you need to say. Then describe one
way to say it with care. Check whether your
proposed wording makes a specific request,
leaves room for a response, and avoids
assigning a motive.
Wait before sending a difficult message
Draft a direct reply to a message that
frustrated you. Read it once and identify
every claim about the sender’s motives.
Replace each claim with a fact you can see
or a question the sender can answer. If the
discussion involves a sensitive relationship,
ask for a private conversation. At the end,
send a brief recap of the time agreed or the
decision made. Keep private details out of
the group thread.
Disagree without making the other person defend their character
Two volunteers remember a planning
conversation differently. One recalls a firm
assignment. The other remembers an
invitation they could decline. A charge such
as “you didn’t keep your word” invites a
defense of character while leaving the
original wording unexamined. Ask each
person what they understood the
assignment to be. If there is a written
message, read it together. If the wording
was ambiguous, acknowledge the
ambiguity and make a clear assignment for
next time.
There may be no way to settle every detail.
A useful agreement can still say that future
requests will include the role, the date, and
a clear way to accept. If you had
responsibility for the original request, name
what you will do differently. You need no verdict on a person’s intention to make the next invitation clearer.
Consider a mild disagreement you can
rehearse safely. Describe it first as a
judgment about someone, then rewrite it as
a difference in what each person
understood. Identify a piece of evidence
that would help, and one future practice
each person can influence even if that
evidence is unavailable.
5 Give care and follow through
Read Romans 12:15 and Galatians 6:2. A
person bringing grief, shame, or
disappointment may need time to speak
before they can consider a practical step.
Ask, “Would you like me to listen a little
longer, pray with you, or help you think
through what comes next?” Give them
room to choose and stay present while they
decide.
CHAPTER 5 · LISTENING IN PRACTICE
Give care and follow through
Accra, Ghana. A friend stops by with groceries and asks what would help next time.
I’m going to the store Thursday. Would it help if I picked something up?
Yes, two items would help. I’ll send you the names.
Offer something the person can accept or decline.
Suppose a member tells you they stopped
attending because they felt alone while
caring for a sick relative. You cannot
change the weeks they spent alone. You
can ask what company or practical help
would serve them now and make a specific
promise you can keep. “Would you like me
to call Thursday evening?” Record the
reminder privately and call when you said
you would. Ask permission before sharing
their situation with a prayer group or
another volunteer.
Seven days of practice
1 — Put away distractions for one
conversation and let the other person
finish.
2 — Ask for a recent example before
responding to a broad complaint.
3 — Reflect back the concern and invite a
correction.
4 — Check the meaning of a message
whose tone you find yourself guessing.
5 — Receive one piece of feedback and
name one point you can verify.
6 — Ask what kind of support would help
before offering advice or prayer.
7 — Keep a promise you made in
conversation and record what you learned.
At the end of the week, choose one
relationship in which you want to become
more dependable. Name one recurring
moment when listening tends to break
down, such as the first five minutes after
work or the final minutes of a volunteer
meeting. Choose one practice to bring into
that moment next week.
Prayer. Father, make me quick to hear,
patient when I am corrected, and truthful
when I speak. Teach me to keep the
promises I make and to offer care with
humility. Amen.
Follow through without taking over
A person asks you to check in after a
difficult week. Agree on a day, the kind of
contact they prefer, and any specific help
you can provide. If they ask you to keep the
conversation private, explain any limits that
apply before they share further. Ask
permission before involving someone else
when that is appropriate. When danger or
abuse is disclosed, take protective action in
accordance with applicable safeguarding
procedures.
During the follow-up, begin with the
question you promised to ask. “How did the
appointment go, and how are you doing
today?” Let them choose how much to
share. If they want ongoing practical help,
clarify who will do what. A short, specific
agreement prevents an offer of support
from becoming another task they have to
manage alone.
Personal practice plan. Name the
relationship in which you want to listen
better, the recurring conversation where
you will practice, and the words you want to
try. Choose a date to reflect on what
changed. Invite feedback with a question
someone can answer, such as “Was there a
moment when you felt I understood what
you were saying?”
Receive a correction in front of others
A volunteer corrects the time you
announced in a meeting. Acknowledge the
correction and check the event record. If
the record confirms their correction, thank
them and update the people who heard the
first time. If the record is unclear, give the
team a time when you will send the
confirmed answer. Check how it felt to be
corrected. That feeling can inform your
prayer without deciding how you speak to
the volunteer.
Offer support that the person can accept or decline
Someone who is caring for a sick relative
may be grateful for concern and too tired to
coordinate help. “Let me know if you need
anything” asks them to imagine
possibilities, decide which requests are
reasonable, and contact you again. An offer
of one specific action is easier to accept.
“I’m going to the grocery store Thursday.
Would it help if I picked up two items for
you?” Give them room to decline or suggest
a different time.
When they ask for prayer, ask whether they
want you to pray with them now or in
private. If you are asked to share a request,
agree what words and audience are
appropriate. A general request can
sometimes meet the need without including
personal details. If the person describes a
situation requiring protective action, use
the appropriate safeguarding route.
Keep track of practical commitments in a
way that protects privacy. If a grocery
delivery is agreed for Thursday, confirm
where to leave it and send a brief update if
plans change. Next time you speak, ask
whether the delivery helped and what
would be convenient going forward. Good
care fits the life the other person is actually
living.
6 Listen when the conversation starts in writing
Read Proverbs 18:17. The first version you
hear of an event can shape everything that
follows. The same thing happens when you
read a message in a tone the writer never
intended. Put the words and your
interpretation side by side. “Fine, I’ll handle
it” is the text. “They resent me” is one
possible interpretation. A practical first step
is to ask what the sender needs to finish the
work.
At home, someone texts that they will
make dinner themselves. You might read it
as criticism because you are already
worried about being late. Reply with the
fact you can confirm and a short question.
“I’m still at work and expect to be home by
seven. Is there something you’d like me to
pick up on the way?” If the response opens
a larger concern, suggest a spoken
CHAPTER 6 · LISTENING IN PRACTICE
Listen when the conversation starts in writing
Chengdu, China. A reader pauses before replying to a brief message.
“Fine, I’ll handle it.” What do those words actually tell me?
Do you have what you need, or did we miss something?
Check the practical concern before responding to an assumed tone.
conversation and agree on a time. Leave
the text thread with one useful decision.
When a group message needs a private reply
A church team receives a note about
missed duties. A volunteer replies that
another member let them down. The
coordinator can acknowledge the
scheduling issue in the group and speak
individually about the disagreement. “We
still need someone to cover the door at
nine. I’ll handle the schedule here and
check privately on what happened.” In the
private conversation, ask permission before
relaying personal information.
Exercise. Choose one message you have
been tempted to answer sharply. Write
three things in separate sentences. What
does the message actually say? What tone
did you assign? What question could clarify
the task? Read your reply once as though you received it without knowing your own intentions.
Decide what belongs in writing
A team chat is useful for announcing a
schedule that everyone needs. It is a poor
place to debate why one person missed a
shift. If a coordinator addresses the
absence in front of the group, others may
join without knowing what happened. Post
the coverage need in the group, and ask
the person privately whether they received
the assignment and what prevented them
from attending. The private conversation
can reveal a forwarding problem or a
difficulty they would not have discussed
publicly.
When a voice note contains several
requests, write a short response naming
what you heard, what you can do, and what
still needs to be discussed. If one request is
unclear, ask about it specifically. A long
reply to a long message can leave both people unsure whether the question at the end was answered. Place the decision first if others are waiting on it.
Before sending a correction, ask who needs
to read it. Correct the schedule for
everyone who received the wrong version.
Send personal feedback directly to the
person involved. In your own group, identify
one kind of message that regularly gets too
much attention. Propose a quieter channel
for it and agree who will summarize any
decision back to the people affected.
Pick the right channel
Group note Private talk Shared decision
Publish shared logistics, speak privately about personal friction.
7 Make it easier for different people to contribute
Read Romans 12:10 and 12:16. Giving
honor can mean changing how a
conversation is organized. A person who
prefers time to think may contribute little
when a question is asked without warning.
Someone who has difficulty following
overlapping speech may lose the thread of
a lively meeting. A group can invite fuller
participation by sharing the question ahead
of time, taking turns, and offering a written
option.
CHAPTER 7 · LISTENING IN PRACTICE
Make room for other contributions
Bangkok, Thailand. A meeting participant hands her written input to the facilitator.
You can share your answer aloud or give me a written note.
I’d like the group to check the walk from the bus stop.
Give people a workable way to contribute before the decision.
A decision with information that arrived late
A committee is comparing two community
event locations. One participant nods
during the meeting and later emails
concerns about the entrances. The chair
initially assumes that objections raised
after the meeting are an attempt to reopen
a settled choice. Ask when the participant
received the site details and whether the
group had the information before the vote.
If the details only arrived afterward, identify
which part of the decision needs
reconsidering.
Agree on what every reviewer will receive
and when comments are due. When a
deadline is tight, state it plainly and explain
the consequence. “We need to confirm the
venue by Friday. Please send any access
issue we should consider before Thursday
at noon.” This is easier to act on than a
general request to send thoughts soon.
Exercise. Find one regular conversation
where the same voices answer first.
Change one element at the next meeting.
Share the question early, invite a written
answer, or give people an uninterrupted
turn. Ask someone who normally speaks
less whether the change helped them
contribute.
Follow up after a pastoral conversation
After receiving a request for prayer, ask
whether the person wants a private
follow-up and how they want to receive it.
When you call, begin by asking how they
are doing since you last spoke. Let them
share at their own pace. If they request
help outside your role, agree on whom to
contact or what information they need.
Record the promise in a private way and
follow through. Review whether the support
you offered matched the request they
actually made.
Hear the person who cannot answer on the spot
In a neighborhood planning group,
someone is asked whether the event venue
works for everyone. They cannot know until
they have seen where the bus stops and
how far the walk is. A fast answer may
sound confident while overlooking a barrier.
Share the address, timing and transport
information in advance. Invite comments
with a clear deadline and say which parts of
the plan can still be changed.
Some people respond best orally, some
after writing down their thoughts, and some
after reviewing documents. Offer a practical
alternative where it is possible. You can
provide a short summary or accept a
private note. The purpose is to improve the
decision, so review late-arriving concerns
according to whether the information was
available earlier and what the group can
still act on.
After your next group discussion, compare
the concerns raised aloud with the concerns
submitted later. Ask why a meaningful
issue only appeared after the meeting. If
the information came late, provide it earlier
next time. If the person feared
embarrassment, consider collecting
individual input before asking everyone to
discuss the issue in public.
8 Follow an agreement through to the next conversation
Read James 1:22 and Matthew 5:37. An
honest conversation can end with a broad
promise such as “I’ll do better.” Make the
next step clear enough for both people to
recognize it. Include who will act, when, and
how the other person will hear about it.
When the agreement involves someone
else, check that person’s availability before
making a promise on their behalf.
CHAPTER 8 · LISTENING IN PRACTICE
Follow an agreement through
Ibadan, Nigeria. Family members use a calendar to agree on a household task.
We need dinner before the evening appointment. What time works?
I can have it ready at six. I’ll message you if that changes.
Record the time and check later whether the agreement helped.
Make a small promise you can keep
Two relatives want to discuss housework
after dinner. One expects to settle the
whole week’s schedule and the other has
time for ten minutes. Agree that each
person will name one concern. Choose a
small task to change this week and decide
when to revisit the schedule. Starting with
one action can make it easier to see
whether the arrangement helps.
At the next conversation, ask about the
action you agreed on. If it did not happen,
describe what prevented it and ask what
adjustment would be realistic. Then decide
who will act and when. A new agreement is
useful when it accounts for the reason the
first one failed.
Practice record. Write your agreement in
one sentence, give it a date, and put the
date where you will see it. At the follow-up,
record what you did, what the other person experienced, and whether the next step needs to change.
Closing prayer. Father, help me hear what
people are trying to tell me and keep the
commitments I make. Give me a gentle
voice, a teachable spirit and the patience to
follow through. Amen.
Check the effect of an agreement
A couple agrees that one person will handle
meals on Thursday. They complete the
meal, but make it an hour later than the
other person expected. The task was
performed and the timing still failed the
household. In the follow-up conversation,
ask which part mattered and whether it had
been clearly agreed. If the real need is to
eat before an evening appointment, put
that condition into the next agreement.
When you cannot keep a commitment,
notify the other person before they have to
discover it themselves. Name the part you
can still do and ask whether the proposed change serves the purpose. “I can bring the supplies Friday, but I know you said setup was Thursday. Can I arrange delivery
Thursday instead?” The question
distinguishes your preferred solution from
the other person’s actual need.
Choose a modest commitment to review a
week from now. Put the task and time in a
place both people can check. In the
follow-up, ask what worked and what
adjustment would make it easier to sustain.
If the commitment no longer serves
anyone, give it a clear ending instead of
carrying it forward out of habit.
Agree and review
Say the task Choose a time Check the result
A usable commitment names the action, owner and date.
Putting listening into practice together
Slow down an argument without avoiding it
Two people may both be trying to resolve a
disagreement while speaking from different
moments in the story. One wants to
describe a promise made last week. The
other wants to decide what happens
tomorrow. When they take turns on
different questions, each person can feel
ignored even though both are speaking
honestly. Ask which question they want
heard first. Agree on how long each person
gets to speak, and write down the other
question so it has a place when the first is
finished.
Begin with the part you can state
accurately. “You expected a message
before the plan changed, and when it came
afterward you had already made

arrangements.” Ask whether that sentence captures what happened. Then tell the other person which concern you want them to hear. If you disagree about a detail, narrow the disagreement to the detail instead of making it a verdict on the person. “I remember giving a tentative date. You remember me confirming it. Let’s check the message together.”
A pause can be a responsible decision when
someone cannot continue calmly. Explain
when and how you will return, if it is safe
and appropriate to do so. Pray privately for
patience and clarity during the break. When
you return, begin with the unresolved
question. If the conversation repeatedly
involves intimidation or someone
reasonably fears harm, seek appropriate
help and put safety first.
Listen in a group where some voices carry more weight
At a church meeting a respected volunteer
answers every question quickly. Others
agree immediately, but an issue appears in
private afterward. Before the next meeting,
circulate the actual decision to be made.
Give everyone the same information,
including what can still change and what
has already been decided. Invite people to
read the material ahead or bring an answer
in writing. Those options can help people
who need more time decide whether they
have something to contribute.
During the meeting, distinguish a question
of fact from a question of preference. “Can
we afford the room?” requires a confirmed
figure. “Which room will make the group
more comfortable?” calls for different
experiences. Ask the people who have to
carry out the decision what they would
need. Summarize the concerns before
announcing what will happen. When a decision goes against a recommendation, name the reason and thank the person for making the group aware of it.
Read 1 Corinthians 12:14–26 as a group
leader. Paul describes interdependence
rather than a competition among members
of the body. Consider whose burden
becomes visible only when you ask how a
decision will affect them. After the meeting,
invite one person who did not speak to say
whether the arrangement gave them a fair
way to contribute. Respect their choice
about answering.
Receive a story without turning it into a verdict
When a friend says someone treated them
badly, your first task may be to understand
what the experience was like for them. Ask
what happened and what they need now.
You can acknowledge pain without deciding
facts you have no way to confirm. Reflect
their own words and clarify any practical
concern that affects the next step. If a
concern requires a formal report, tell them
what process applies before acting where
that is appropriate.
Proverbs 18:17 offers a useful restraint
when you are asked to decide a dispute.
The first account may seem complete until
more is known. Seek the information you
need, use the proper channel, and keep the
details limited to people who have a role. A
private concern can become harder to
resolve if it travels ahead of the people
involved. Ask what can be shared, with whom and for what purpose, taking account of any safeguarding obligations.
Practice a neutral summary. “I heard that
the conversation happened after the
meeting and that the change was
unexpected. I need to check when
everyone received the schedule.” That
sentence takes the speaker seriously and
gives a concrete next step. Write your own
version for a mild disagreement. Remove
any phrase that suggests you already know
another person’s motives.
Hear grief at its own pace
Someone who is grieving may tell the same
part of a story on two occasions. The
meaning may be different the second time.
The first account might describe an event.
The next might reveal what they miss most.
Give the person space to speak without
correcting the order or pressing for more
detail. If they prefer to sit quietly, your
presence can be enough for that visit.
Romans 12:15 calls believers to weep with
those who weep. A question such as “How
has this week been for you?” gives the
person room to choose what to share. If
they say mornings are especially difficult,
ask whether there is a small and specific
kind of support they would welcome. An
offer to call at a chosen time is more useful
than a broad promise of availability that
you cannot maintain. Ask before praying
aloud or passing along a request.
After a visit, consider whether you gave the
person room to own their choices. Write a
brief prayer asking God to give you
patience. If you promised a call, put it on
your calendar and keep it. A dependable
act of care can communicate that the
person was heard even when you have no
answer for the loss itself.
Practice a difficult conversation in three rounds
Choose an ordinary conflict the participants
are comfortable rehearsing. It could involve
a changed pickup time at home or a
volunteer assignment that arrived late. In
the first round, let one person explain the
situation for a minute. The listener reflects
one verified fact and one concern. The
speaker identifies anything the listener
missed. Write down the correction in a
single sentence.
In the second round, the listener asks a
question that would separate an event from
an interpretation. “When did you receive
the message?” can establish the event.
“What made the timing difficult for you?”
invites the effect. Give the speaker time to
supply both. Together, decide whether the
question helped or felt like a challenge.
Adjust tense words or assumptions before
trying it again.
In the third round, decide on a small action.
Say who will do it, when it will happen, and
what to do if timing changes. Each person
should be able to repeat the agreement
accurately. End by naming one difference
between the first round and the third. Read
James 1:19 again and identify one place to
practice the same restraint this week.
Hold a four week review
In the first week, notice when you are most
likely to interrupt. Pick one repeatable
change, such as putting your phone away
at the table. In the second week, work on
questions. Ask for the latest specific
example before making a broad conclusion.
In the third week, practice reflecting a
concern and inviting correction in one
conversation where the outcome matters
but the relationship is safe. In the fourth
week, check your follow-through by
reviewing a promise you made and asking
whether you kept it in the way the other
person expected.
Use one page of a private notebook for
each week. Record what happened, what
you thought at the time, and what the other
person later clarified. Leave out identifying
details that you have no reason to keep.
When you see a repeated mistake, choose
one new practice instead of trying to
overhaul the whole relationship. Ask a
trusted person whether your change is
visible in everyday conversation.
Close with prayer. Ask for a heart that can
receive correction, for courage to say
truthful words gently, and for wisdom about
which burdens are yours to carry. Choose
one commitment to keep after the four
weeks finish. Write it in language that a
family member, coworker or fellow church
member can understand.
